meta.title: Search Autocomplete
meta.summary: Suggest popular completions on every keystroke from a precomputed in-memory trie, rebuilt from search logs every hour.

functional: Return the top 10 completions for a typed prefix
Trending queries show up within about an hour
nonFunctional: < 100 ms p99 per keystroke, including the network

scale.label: Edge hit ratio
scale.value: ~80% of suggest requests answered by the CDN, so ~230k/s reach the origin at the ~1.2M/s peak

slos.name: Suggestion speed
slos.sli: Suggest requests answered within the threshold, divided by all, measured in the browser (real-user timing beacons) so the network is included; the CDN's own timing is the fast proxy for alerts

slos.name: Suggest availability
slos.sli: Suggest requests that succeed (not 5xx or timeout) divided by all suggest requests, measured at the CDN

slos.name: Trend freshness
slos.sli: Queries that enter the hourly top 1,000 in the aggregator and appear in a served trie within the threshold, divided by all such queries, checked by comparing aggregator output with the loaded trie version

alerts.when: Suggest errors burning the error budget 14 times too fast over 1 hour and over 5 minutes (a slow burn, 6 times over 6 hours, opens a ticket)
alerts.why: Search feels broken without suggestions, even though search itself still works.

alerts.when: p99 latency above 100 ms for 10 minutes
alerts.why: Suggestions must keep up with typing, or they are worse than none.
The hourly rebuild or the rollout is failing, and suggestions grow stale.

alerts.when: CDN hit ratio below 80% for 30 minutes
alerts.why: The origin is sized for about 80% edge hits (~230k/s at peak); below that the Suggest Service runs out of headroom.

alerts.when: Trie build failed, or took over twice its normal time
alerts.why: Fix before the next rebuild, or the trie goes stale.

alerts.when: Aggregator lag behind the search log above 20 minutes for 30 minutes
alerts.why: Counts arrive late, so the next hourly build misses trending queries even if it succeeds.

signals.name: Trie version age
signals.why: The direct measure of how stale suggestions are.

signals.name: Build duration and output size
signals.why: A sudden size drop usually means broken input, not fewer queries.

signals.name: Suggestion click-through
signals.why: The business measure: the share of searches that used a suggestion. A drop after a rollout means the new trie is worse even if nothing errors.

steps: Check the trie version age on each serving node.
Check the last builder run and its output size.
Check how far the aggregator lags behind the search log.
Roll back to the previous snapshot if the new one is bad.

nodes.label: WAF
nodes.description: Attached to the CDN distribution: managed rule sets, per-IP rate rules and bot control against scrapers harvesting suggestions

nodes.label: DNS
nodes.description: Points the search hostname at the WAF-protected CDN distribution

nodes.label: CDN
nodes.description: Caches responses per normalized prefix and language for a few minutes; ignores cookies, so one cached answer serves everyone

nodes.label: Search Service
nodes.description: Runs the search itself (outside this design's scope); emits one event per submitted search

nodes.label: Suggest Service
nodes.description: Holds the whole trie in memory; top-10 precomputed at every node, stored as ids into a shared string table because those lists dominate memory. 20 instances carry the ~230k/s origin peak at ~20k/s each with headroom

nodes.label: Query Counts
nodes.description: query → popularity score and the hour it was last updated (decay applied lazily)

nodes.label: Search Log
nodes.description: One event per submitted search, never per keystroke

nodes.label: Aggregator
nodes.description: Counts queries per window and applies time decay; one write per query per window

flows.title: Keystroke (cache hit)
flows.summary: Most prefixes are short and popular, so the CDN answers without reaching the origin.

steps.label: resolve search.example.com
steps.detail: Cached by the browser and by resolvers, so the lookup happens once per session and autocomplete keystrokes never wait on DNS.

steps.label: debounce 100 ms
steps.detail: Wait until typing pauses briefly. Fast typists send far fewer requests.

steps.label: inspect, then pass
steps.detail: Per-IP rate rules and bot control stop scrapers that walk every prefix to copy the suggestion list. A WAF is priced per request, so at ~50B requests a day it is a real cost line; the rules are kept to the few that matter.

steps.label: HIT (max-age 300)
steps.detail: The cache key is the normalized prefix (lowercased, spaces collapsed) plus language, with no cookies, so one entry serves everyone. Prefix popularity follows a power law, so a few thousand short prefixes cover most traffic.

flows.title: Keystroke (cache miss)
flows.summary: A longer, rarer prefix reaches the origin, where one trie walk returns the precomputed answer.

steps.label: forward to origin
steps.detail: The edge adds a request id that the load balancer and the Suggest Service log and trace, so one slow keystroke can be followed end to end.

steps.label: walk trie, read top-10
steps.detail: Each trie node stores its own top-10 list, so the lookup costs O(length of prefix). No subtree search, no database.

steps.label: top 10
steps.detail: Now cached at this edge for the next five minutes.

flows.title: Hourly trie rebuild
flows.summary: Popularity is computed offline; serving nodes swap to a new snapshot without downtime.

steps.label: searched "system design"
steps.detail: Only submitted searches feed popularity, so the Search Service, not the Suggest Service, writes the log. Keystrokes are never logged.

steps.label: upsert decayed scores
steps.detail: Counts are summed per query over the window first, so a viral query is one write per window, not millions. Each row stores its score and the hour it was updated; decay is applied when the row is next written or read (score × decay^hours since), so idle queries fade without rewriting every row each hour.
steps.payload:
UpdateItem q='system design'
SET score = <old score × 0.9^3> + 1840, updated_hour = '2026-11-10T14'

steps.label: parallel scan, keep top 100M
steps.detail: A full parallel scan once an hour, applying each row's decay and keeping the best 100M queries in a heap.

steps.label: build trie, top-k per node
steps.detail: Also filters offensive and policy-blocked phrases before they can be suggested.

steps.label: load trie-v1234 (rolling)
steps.detail: After the builder's checks pass (size, sample lookups), instances load the new version a few at a time and swap atomically in memory, so each needs room for two copies while it loads. Rolling back is loading the previous snapshot.

notes.text: If the trie no longer fits in one machine's memory, shard by prefix range (a-f, g-m, …) and route by first characters. Memory, not CPU, decides the instance type, which is why it runs on containers with large memory rather than a platform with a small memory cap.
Caching responses for 5 minutes removes most origin load at the cost of a few minutes of staleness, which suggestions tolerate.
Offline rebuilds keep the serving path read-only and simple. Real-time trending needs a second, small, frequently updated trie merged at query time.
Serving nodes are stateless after loading a snapshot; a failed node is replaced and loads the latest version.
Personalization (your own recent searches) is usually a separate small per-user list merged in on the client or at the service.

The WAF stops scrapers harvesting the suggestion list and floods that try to push a query into suggestions by searching it from many clients; the second also needs per-user and per-IP de-duplication in the aggregator before counting. Queries feeding global suggestions are stripped of user ids, and the builder's blocklist keeps personal data and offensive phrases out of the trie.

questions.q: Suggestions must appear within about 100 ms of each keystroke. Where does that time budget go?
questions.a: Serve from memory: the suggest service holds the trie for the top prefixes, so a lookup is microseconds. Cache popular prefix responses at the CDN and in the browser, and debounce keystrokes on the client. The rebuilt trie is loaded from a snapshot, never queried from a database on the hot path.

questions.q: A breaking news term should start appearing in suggestions. How fresh can they be?
questions.a: The batch pipeline rebuilds the trie hourly, which is fine for most terms. For trending terms add a small fast path: a streaming counter over recent minutes whose top terms are merged into the results at query time. Freshness is a trade-off against cost and stability.

questions.q: How do you decide which completions to show for a prefix?
questions.a: Rank by query frequency with time decay so recent popularity counts more, and store the top K completions at every trie node so a lookup does not have to search the subtree. Personal history can be blended on the client or in a separate step. Filter offensive or unsafe terms before they enter the trie.

questions.q: The trie no longer fits in one server's memory. What do you do?
questions.a: Shard it by prefix range, for example by the first one or two characters, with a routing table that balances popular ranges. Each shard is replicated for availability. Trimming rare queries from the trie usually shrinks it a lot before sharding is needed.

questions.q: How do you roll out a newly built trie safely?
questions.a: Write the new snapshot alongside the old one, validate it (size, sample lookups), then have servers load it in the background and switch atomically. Keep the previous snapshot so you can roll back instantly if suggestions look wrong.

questions.q: Every keystroke could be logged. How do you keep the logging volume sane?
questions.a: Log completed searches, not keystrokes: the Search Service emits one event per submitted search, and the Suggest Service logs nothing per keystroke. Sample if needed, since ranking only needs relative frequencies, and aggregate counts per window rather than writing one row per query. Drop personal data from what feeds the global suggestions.
